html.title: Build your first HTML page
html.body:
HTML describes the structure of a page. A heading uses

, a paragraph uses

, and a link uses . Opening and closing tags wrap the content. The href attribute tells the browser where a link goes. Start with one clear heading and a short paragraph. Use descriptive link text so people know where it leads. Your page should still make sense without colours or images.
html.practice: Write HTML for a page about yourself: one h1, a p about your interests, and an a linking to a useful website. Explain what href does.
html.statement: HTML describes the structure of a web page.

css.title: Style a page with CSS
css.body:
CSS controls presentation: colour, spacing and layout. A selector chooses an element; declarations inside braces set properties. In h1 { color: green; }, h1 is the selector and color is the property.
Use readable text, enough contrast and flexible widths. A fixed width of 900px can overflow a phone screen. max-width: 100% helps content fit. Keep the heading structure from your HTML.
css.practice: Write CSS to give your heading a colour and your paragraph some padding. Explain why a page should fit a small screen.
css.statement: CSS replaces the need for HTML page structure.
css.code:
h1 { color: green; }
p { padding: 16px; max-width: 100%; }

javascript.title: Add interaction with JavaScript
javascript.body:
JavaScript responds to actions and changes page behaviour. querySelector finds an element; addEventListener runs a function when an event occurs. textContent changes text without treating it as HTML.
A button already supports keyboard interaction. Use a real button rather than a clickable paragraph. Keep the page useful before the script loads.
javascript.practice: Write a button and a JavaScript click listener that changes a paragraph to a welcome message. Explain which event starts the change.
javascript.statement: A click event listener can respond when a button is activated.

data.title: Turn data into a useful question
data.body: Data is recorded information. Start with a question, then organise observations into rows and fields into columns. Missing values are not the same as zero. Check units and repeated rows before calculating. An average is the sum divided by the number of values.
data.practice: Use these daily sales: 10, 20, 30. Calculate the average, label the unit, and write one question the numbers cannot answer.

cyber.title: Protect an account
cyber.body: A password protects access to an account. Use a unique password for each service and a password manager to store it. Multi-factor authentication adds another check. Unexpected messages asking for a password or code may be phishing. Open the service directly to verify a request.
cyber.practice: Describe how you would check an unexpected login message. List two steps to protect a test account; do not enter any real passwords here.
cyber.statement: It is safe to send a sign-in code to anyone who claims to be support.

ai.title: Understand a model prediction
ai.body: A machine learning model learns patterns from examples. Training data influences its predictions. A prediction can be wrong, especially when new examples differ from the training data. Evaluate on separate examples and compare errors, not just successes.
ai.practice: Imagine a model recognising fruit. Describe examples for training and separate examples for testing. Name one situation where it might fail.
ai.statement: A model prediction is guaranteed to be correct.

design.title: Design around a user need
design.body: User experience starts with a person and a goal. Describe the problem before drawing screens. A clear label helps people choose the right action. A simple sketch can be tested before building. Observe where someone gets stuck rather than assuming what they need.
design.practice: Sketch a three-step flow for saving a lesson. Name the user goal and one question you would ask during a test.
design.statement: Testing a sketch can reveal problems before an app is built.

marketing.title: Plan a useful message
marketing.body: Marketing connects a useful offer with an audience. Define who you want to reach, what problem you solve and what action you want them to take. Measure a relevant outcome, such as enquiries, rather than relying only on views. Avoid claims you cannot support.
marketing.practice: Write a short message for a local service. Identify its audience, benefit and one clear action. Choose a measure of success.
marketing.statement: More views always mean more customers.

business.title: Test a business idea
business.body: A business idea needs a customer problem and a workable offer. Talk to potential customers before investing heavily. Revenue is money received; profit also accounts for costs. A small test can reveal whether people value your offer.
business.practice: An item sells for 100 and costs 70 to provide. Calculate the difference before other costs, then describe a small customer test.
business.statement: Costs need to be considered when estimating profit.

writing.title: Write for a reader
writing.body: Clear writing has a purpose and an audience. Put the main point early, use concrete words and give the reader a next step. Revise sentences that combine too many ideas. Check whether the reader has enough context to act.
writing.practice: Write a four-sentence message inviting a friend to a study session. Include the purpose, time, place and next action.
writing.statement: Knowing your audience helps you decide what details to include.

project.title: Break a project into tasks
project.body: A project has an outcome, tasks and constraints. Break work into small tasks, assign responsibility and identify dependencies. A task that needs another task first cannot start freely. Review progress and adjust the plan when circumstances change.
project.practice: Plan a small study event with four tasks, an owner for each and one dependency. State what a successful event would achieve.
project.statement: Every project task can always start at the same time.

teaching.title: Help someone learn
teaching.body: A lesson needs a clear learning goal, an example, practice and feedback. Demonstrating a skill is not the same as learning it. Ask the learner to try the skill and explain their reasoning. Use the response to decide what to teach next.
teaching.practice: Plan a ten-minute lesson on a skill you know. Write its goal, a practice activity and one question to check understanding.
teaching.statement: Practice and feedback help a teacher check understanding.

web-semantic.title: Use semantic HTML
web-semantic.body:
Use header for introductory content, main for the page’s central content and footer for closing information.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
web-semantic.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Use semantic HTML”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-semantic.statement: Use header for introductory content, main for the page’s central content and footer for closing information.

web-layout.title: Build responsive layouts
web-layout.body:
Grid auto-fit creates as many columns as fit; minmax prevents cards becoming too narrow.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
web-layout.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Build responsive layouts”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-layout.statement: The most attractive option is always the best for every goal.
web-layout.code: .cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }

web-forms.title: Collect input with forms
web-forms.body:
A label names its input; type=email checks format and required rejects an empty value.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.
web-forms.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Collect input with forms”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-forms.statement: A label names its input; type=email checks format and required rejects an empty value.

web-dom.title: Connect events to the DOM
web-dom.body:
querySelector finds an element; addEventListener connects an action to a function; textContent changes plain text.

Some steps depend on earlier steps. Follow the arrows in the worked example and explain what must happen first and why. A sequence should also describe what happens when a step fails. Check each transition before moving on; completing the last step alone does not prove the whole process worked.
web-dom.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Connect events to the DOM”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-dom.statement: A dependent step can always start before its prerequisite.

web-access.title: Make a page accessible
web-access.body:
Real buttons support keyboard activation. Text needs sufficient contrast, and actions need descriptive labels.

Feedback is useful when it refers to an observation and suggests a specific next step. Inspect the example for evidence of what worked and what caused difficulty. Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Make one improvement and check whether it helps; a small sample does not represent everyone.
web-access.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Make a page accessible”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-access.statement: Real buttons support keyboard activation. Text needs sufficient contrast, and actions need descriptive labels.

web-debug.title: Debug and test a feature
web-debug.body:
Test normal and zero quantities; a multiplication function should return 15 for 5 × 3 and zero for 5 × 0.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.
web-debug.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Debug and test a feature”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-debug.statement: Testing only one successful case proves a feature works in all situations.

web-project.title: Build a personal website
web-project.body:
Combine semantic HTML, responsive CSS and one keyboard-accessible interaction in your personal website.

Bring the earlier skills together in a small project. Use the worked example as a starting outline, define a useful outcome and create something you can demonstrate. Test it against your goal, explain a limitation and record one improvement. Keep your draft and evidence so another learner can understand your decisions.
web-project.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Build a personal website”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
web-project.statement: Combine semantic HTML, responsive CSS and one keyboard-accessible interaction in your personal website.

data-clean.title: Clean a small dataset
data-clean.body:
A repeated identifier may be a duplicate. An empty value is unknown, not automatically zero.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
data-clean.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Clean a small dataset”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-clean.statement: A repeated identifier may be a duplicate. An empty value is unknown, not automatically zero.

data-measures.title: Choose useful summary measures
data-measures.body:
Mean uses all values and is sensitive to extremes; median is the middle of sorted values.

A calculation needs defined inputs, an operation and a meaningful unit. Work through the example by hand before using a tool. Check the denominator, missing values and whether the result is plausible. An accurate calculation still needs context before it supports a decision.
data-measures.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Choose useful summary measures”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-measures.statement: The units and denominator do not matter in a calculation.

data-sheets.title: Calculate with spreadsheets
data-sheets.body:
SUM adds a range, AVERAGE finds its mean and COUNT counts its numeric cells.

A calculation needs defined inputs, an operation and a meaningful unit. Work through the example by hand before using a tool. Check the denominator, missing values and whether the result is plausible. An accurate calculation still needs context before it supports a decision.
data-sheets.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Calculate with spreadsheets”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-sheets.statement: SUM adds a range, AVERAGE finds its mean and COUNT counts its numeric cells.

data-filter.title: Sort and filter records
data-filter.body:
Filtering keeps matching rows; sorting changes row order without changing the recorded values.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
data-filter.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Sort and filter records”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-filter.statement: The most attractive option is always the best for every goal.

data-charts.title: Choose an honest chart
data-charts.body:
Bar charts compare categories. Label units and start a bar’s numerical axis at zero.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
data-charts.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Choose an honest chart”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-charts.statement: Bar charts compare categories. Label units and start a bar’s numerical axis at zero.
data-charts.code:
A: ███ 30
B: ██ 20
C: █ 10
// axis starts at 0; same unit

data-sql.title: Group data with SQL
data-sql.body:
GROUP BY forms groups; SUM calculates one total for each group in the SQL result.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
data-sql.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Group data with SQL”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-sql.statement: Missing information should always be replaced with zero.

data-privacy.title: Handle personal data carefully
data-privacy.body:
Replacing names with IDs reduces exposure, but other fields may still identify a person.

Use invented information for this exercise. Collect only the information needed for a clear purpose, remove identifying details and limit who can see it. The example shows data that should be removed or permission that should be checked. Do not put real passwords, contact details or confidential records in your notes.
data-privacy.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Handle personal data carefully”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-privacy.statement: Replacing names with IDs reduces exposure, but other fields may still identify a person.

data-evidence.title: Explain findings and limits
data-evidence.body:
State sample size and uncertainty. An association between two values does not establish causation.

Feedback is useful when it refers to an observation and suggests a specific next step. Inspect the example for evidence of what worked and what caused difficulty. Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Make one improvement and check whether it helps; a small sample does not represent everyone.
data-evidence.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Explain findings and limits”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-evidence.statement: A small sample proves what every person needs.

data-project.title: Create a small data report
data-project.body:
Answer one question using cleaned data, a labelled chart and a recommendation with stated limitations.

Bring the earlier skills together in a small project. Use the worked example as a starting outline, define a useful outcome and create something you can demonstrate. Test it against your goal, explain a limitation and record one improvement. Keep your draft and evidence so another learner can understand your decisions.
data-project.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Create a small data report”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
data-project.statement: Answer one question using cleaned data, a labelled chart and a recommendation with stated limitations.

cyber-phishing.title: Spot a phishing link
cyber-phishing.body:
Read the actual hostname: example.test.evil.test belongs to evil.test, not example.test.

A risk combines the chance of something happening with the harm it could cause. In the example, compare likelihood and impact, then choose a practical control. Prioritise larger risks and name who will act. A checklist reduces mistakes but cannot guarantee that every threat has disappeared.
cyber-phishing.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Spot a phishing link”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-phishing.statement: Read the actual hostname: example.test.evil.test belongs to evil.test, not example.test.

cyber-privacy.title: Keep sensitive information private
cyber-privacy.body:
Passwords and sign-in codes are secrets; replace them with invented placeholders in reports.

Use invented information for this exercise. Collect only the information needed for a clear purpose, remove identifying details and limit who can see it. The example shows data that should be removed or permission that should be checked. Do not put real passwords, contact details or confidential records in your notes.
cyber-privacy.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Keep sensitive information private”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-privacy.statement: Real passwords should be included in shared practice notes.

cyber-updates.title: Update devices safely
cyber-updates.body:
Back up important data, obtain updates from the official source, restart and confirm the installed version.

Some steps depend on earlier steps. Follow the arrows in the worked example and explain what must happen first and why. A sequence should also describe what happens when a step fails. Check each transition before moving on; completing the last step alone does not prove the whole process worked.
cyber-updates.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Update devices safely”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-updates.statement: Back up important data, obtain updates from the official source, restart and confirm the installed version.
cyber-updates.code: backup → official update → restart → version check

cyber-network.title: Understand a network journey
cyber-network.body:
DNS resolves names. HTTPS protects data in transit but a fraudulent site can also use HTTPS.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
cyber-network.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Understand a network journey”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-network.statement: Missing information should always be replaced with zero.
cyber-network.code:
device → router → DNS → HTTPS server
// HTTPS protects transit; does not guarantee honesty

cyber-permissions.title: Choose minimum permissions
cyber-permissions.body:
Least privilege gives only the permissions needed for the task; admin access carries additional risk.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
cyber-permissions.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Choose minimum permissions”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-permissions.statement: Least privilege gives only the permissions needed for the task; admin access carries additional risk.
cyber-permissions.code:
viewer: read
editor: read + write
admin: read + write + manage
// role = minimum needed

cyber-backup.title: Test a backup and restore
cyber-backup.body:
An untested backup may be unusable. Restore a harmless test file and compare its contents.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.
cyber-backup.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Test a backup and restore”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-backup.statement: Testing only one successful case proves a feature works in all situations.
cyber-backup.code:
3 copies · 2 storage types · 1 off-site
// restore a test file; compare contents

cyber-threats.title: Prioritise security risks
cyber-threats.body:
Likelihood multiplied by impact provides a simple prioritisation score, not a certain prediction.

A risk combines the chance of something happening with the harm it could cause. In the example, compare likelihood and impact, then choose a practical control. Prioritise larger risks and name who will act. A checklist reduces mistakes but cannot guarantee that every threat has disappeared.
cyber-threats.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Prioritise security risks”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-threats.statement: Likelihood multiplied by impact provides a simple prioritisation score, not a certain prediction.

cyber-response.title: Respond to a suspected incident
cyber-response.body:
For a suspected incident, isolate affected equipment, report it and preserve evidence before recovery.

Some steps depend on earlier steps. Follow the arrows in the worked example and explain what must happen first and why. A sequence should also describe what happens when a step fails. Check each transition before moving on; completing the last step alone does not prove the whole process worked.
cyber-response.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Respond to a suspected incident”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-response.statement: A dependent step can always start before its prerequisite.
cyber-response.code:
isolate → report → preserve evidence → recover
// practise only on your own test device

cyber-project.title: Create a security checklist
cyber-project.body:
Document account protection, updates, permissions and a successful backup restore on your own test setup.

Bring the earlier skills together in a small project. Use the worked example as a starting outline, define a useful outcome and create something you can demonstrate. Test it against your goal, explain a limitation and record one improvement. Keep your draft and evidence so another learner can understand your decisions.
cyber-project.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Create a security checklist”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
cyber-project.statement: Document account protection, updates, permissions and a successful backup restore on your own test setup.

ai-data.title: Organise labelled examples
ai-data.body:
Each training row needs relevant input features and a consistent label; check errors and missing examples.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
ai-data.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Organise labelled examples”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-data.statement: Each training row needs relevant input features and a consistent label; check errors and missing examples.

ai-split.title: Separate training and testing
ai-split.body:
Hold out test examples before training; leaking them into training makes the evaluation misleading.

Training examples help a model learn a pattern; separate test examples check whether it works beyond those examples. Keep the test set out of training and compare predictions with known answers. Errors and unfamiliar cases matter. Good performance on a small test does not guarantee reliable performance everywhere.
ai-split.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Separate training and testing”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-split.statement: Using test examples in training gives a fair evaluation.

ai-baseline.title: Compare with a baseline
ai-baseline.body:
An always-A prediction reaches 75% on three A labels and one B; compare models with this baseline.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
ai-baseline.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Compare with a baseline”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-baseline.statement: An always-A prediction reaches 75% on three A labels and one B; compare models with this baseline.

ai-evaluate.title: Measure prediction accuracy
ai-evaluate.body:
Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all predictions; three correct out of four gives 75%.

A calculation needs defined inputs, an operation and a meaningful unit. Work through the example by hand before using a tool. Check the denominator, missing values and whether the result is plausible. An accurate calculation still needs context before it supports a decision.
ai-evaluate.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Measure prediction accuracy”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-evaluate.statement: The units and denominator do not matter in a calculation.

ai-bias.title: Check errors across groups
ai-bias.body:
An overall score can hide poor results for a group; inspect group results and sample sizes.

Feedback is useful when it refers to an observation and suggests a specific next step. Inspect the example for evidence of what worked and what caused difficulty. Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Make one improvement and check whether it helps; a small sample does not represent everyone.
ai-bias.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Check errors across groups”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-bias.statement: An overall score can hide poor results for a group; inspect group results and sample sizes.

ai-prompts.title: Write a structured prompt
ai-prompts.body:
A prompt should define a task, context, output format and constraints; avoid confidential input.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
ai-prompts.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Write a structured prompt”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-prompts.statement: Missing information should always be replaced with zero.
ai-prompts.code: {"task":"summarise","context":"[synthetic text]","format":"3 bullet points","constraint":"use only supplied facts"}

ai-verification.title: Verify generated claims
ai-verification.body:
Generated text can invent facts and sources. Check claims against the original evidence.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.
ai-verification.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Verify generated claims”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-verification.statement: Generated text can invent facts and sources. Check claims against the original evidence.
ai-verification.code:
claim → source → evidence → verified / unknown
// fluent text ≠ proof

ai-privacy.title: Keep private data out of prompts
ai-privacy.body:
Use synthetic or permitted data and remove confidential details before submitting a prompt.

Use invented information for this exercise. Collect only the information needed for a clear purpose, remove identifying details and limit who can see it. The example shows data that should be removed or permission that should be checked. Do not put real passwords, contact details or confidential records in your notes.
ai-privacy.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Keep private data out of prompts”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-privacy.statement: Real passwords should be included in shared practice notes.

ai-project.title: Build a responsible AI experiment
ai-project.body:
Define a question, build a simple baseline, test separate examples and report errors and limitations.

Bring the earlier skills together in a small project. Use the worked example as a starting outline, define a useful outcome and create something you can demonstrate. Test it against your goal, explain a limitation and record one improvement. Keep your draft and evidence so another learner can understand your decisions.
ai-project.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Build a responsible AI experiment”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
ai-project.statement: Define a question, build a simple baseline, test separate examples and report errors and limitations.

design-research.title: Research a user problem
design-research.body:
Ask about a real recent experience and observe obstacles rather than suggesting the answer.

Begin with the person who needs the work and the action they want to take. The example connects a need, a useful response and a next step. Include enough context to make that step clear, use respectful language and avoid unsupported claims. Check the result with someone from the intended audience.
design-research.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Research a user problem”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
design-research.statement: Ask about a real recent experience and observe obstacles rather than suggesting the answer.
design-research.code:
person → goal → obstacle
// observe behaviour; ask open questions

design-flow.title: Map the user journey
design-flow.body:
Map the happy path and an error or offline path so the user can recover.

Some steps depend on earlier steps. Follow the arrows in the worked example and explain what must happen first and why. A sequence should also describe what happens when a step fails. Check each transition before moving on; completing the last step alone does not prove the whole process worked.
design-flow.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Map the user journey”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
design-flow.statement: A dependent step can always start before its prerequisite.

home → lesson → save → confirmation
// also: offline → retry

design-wireframe.title: Sketch a wireframe
design-wireframe.body:
A wireframe organises content and actions before spending time on colour and visual decoration.

A clear structure gives each part a specific role. Read the worked example from top to bottom and identify the input, the important fields and the result. Missing information should be made explicit, not silently invented. Consistent labels make the work easier to check and reuse.
design-wireframe.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Sketch a wireframe”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
design-wireframe.statement: A wireframe organises content and actions before spending time on colour and visual decoration.

design-hierarchy.title: Create a visual hierarchy
design-hierarchy.body:
Heading size, spacing and one primary action help the user identify what matters first.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
design-hierarchy.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Create a visual hierarchy”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
design-hierarchy.statement: The most attractive option is always the best for every goal.
design-hierarchy.code:
H1 > H2 > body

design-access.title: Check accessible design
design-access.body:
Check readable contrast, keyboard operation, visible focus, labels and zoom without hiding content.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.

keyboard: Tab → Enter
zoom: 200%
label + input

design-prototype.body:

design-usability.body:

Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Make one improvement and check whether it helps; a small sample does not represent everyone.

teaching-feedback.title: Give actionable feedback
teaching-feedback.body:
Describe a specific observation and a next improvement, then let the learner retry.

Feedback is useful when it refers to an observation and suggests a specific next step. Inspect the example for evidence of what worked and what caused difficulty. Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Make one improvement and check whether it helps; a small sample does not represent everyone.
teaching-feedback.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Give actionable feedback”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
teaching-feedback.statement: Describe a specific observation and a next improvement, then let the learner retry.

teaching-check.title: Check skill with a new example
teaching-check.body:
Check the same skill using a new example so memorisation alone cannot pass the check.

A useful test states the input and the expected result before checking the actual result. Try the worked example, then include an empty, unexpected or boundary case. Record what happened and make a small correction. Repeat the test after the correction so you know the problem was addressed.
teaching-check.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Check skill with a new example”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
teaching-check.statement: Testing only one successful case proves a feature works in all situations.

teaching-inclusive.title: Make practice inclusive
teaching-inclusive.body:
Offer readable text, diagrams and accessible interaction while preserving the same learning goal.

Compare options against a clear goal rather than choosing the most attractive one. The example shows alternatives or a constraint. Name the trade-off, keep the comparison fair and justify your choice with evidence. A solution that works in one situation may need adjustment in another.
teaching-inclusive.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Make practice inclusive”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
teaching-inclusive.statement: Offer readable text, diagrams and accessible interaction while preserving the same learning goal.
teaching-inclusive.code:
text + diagram + keyboard access
// same goal; different ways to practise

teaching-plan.title: Plan a short learning session
teaching-plan.body:
Allocate time for a goal, example, learner practice and a check with feedback.

Some steps depend on earlier steps. Follow the arrows in the worked example and explain what must happen first and why. A sequence should also describe what happens when a step fails. Check each transition before moving on; completing the last step alone does not prove the whole process worked.
teaching-plan.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Plan a short learning session”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
teaching-plan.statement: A dependent step can always start before its prerequisite.
teaching-plan.code:
2 min: goal
3 min: example
7 min: practice
3 min: check + feedback

teaching-project.title: Deliver and reflect on a mini lesson
teaching-project.body:
Teach a short session, keep evidence of the learner’s attempt and revise the part that caused difficulty.

Bring the earlier skills together in a small project. Use the worked example as a starting outline, define a useful outcome and create something you can demonstrate. Test it against your goal, explain a limitation and record one improvement. Keep your draft and evidence so another learner can understand your decisions.
teaching-project.practice: Study the example, then create your own version of “Deliver and reflect on a mini lesson”. Change one input or decision, describe the result, and explain why your approach meets the goal.
teaching-project.statement: Teach a short session, keep evidence of the learner’s attempt and revise the part that caused difficulty.
teaching-project.code: goal → starting check → example → practice → feedback → reflection
